highlights: Bosphorus-front urban resort with pine-grove gardens, yachtlike interiors and lavish hammam rituals
description:
Mandarin Oriental, Istanbul sits on the European shore of the Bosphorus in Kuruçeşme, between the residential calm of Bebek and the historic quarters of Beşiktaş. Framed by the Naile Sultan pine grove and the waterway that divides Europe and Asia, the hotel has the rare mood of a resort inside the city, with boat-access perspectives on Ortaköy, Dolmabahçe and the strait’s yali mansions close at hand. Nişantaşı shopping, Beşiktaş museums and the ferries of the European shore are also easily reached.

The 100 rooms and suites pair contemporary Mandarin Oriental polish with restrained Ottoman references: warm wood, bronze accents, discreet patterning and terraces or balconies that draw the gardens and water into the interiors. Tihany Design’s work gives the low-rise property a refined, yachtlike softness rather than palace drama, while the waterfront architecture keeps the focus firmly on the Bosphorus and its changing light.

Dining is arranged around the shore. Novikov Istanbul brings Italian, Asian and Mediterranean inflections to seafood-led cooking; Olea & Bar focuses on Italian gastronomy; and Bosphorus Lounge, its cabanas and the Mandarin Cake Shop cover afternoon tea, patisserie, cocktails and long view-rich afternoons. The mood shifts naturally from waterside lunch to dressed-up evening terrace.

Wellness is a defining feature, with an expansive spa, indoor pool, hammams, sauna, rainforest showers and fitness facilities, while families have connecting-room options and children’s facilities. Gardens, piers, waterfront pools and swift access to Kuruçeşme, Bebek, Ortaköy and the old city give the hotel a poised balance between Istanbul spectacle and retreat-like composure. A private-pier sensibility keeps the water present in both leisure and arrival rituals.

highlights: Jewelled Mayfair hideaway with rooftop cocktails, gallery-rich surroundings and serene subterranean wellness
description:
Mandarin Oriental Mayfair occupies 22 Hanover Square, a poised address between Bond Street and Regent Street where Mayfair’s galleries, auction houses, tailors and jewellery salons gather within a few blocks. The Royal Academy of Arts, Savile Row, Green Park and the West End sit close by, yet the square gives the hotel a more discreet rhythm than London’s larger grand hotels.

Opened as a contemporary boutique-scale counterpart to the brand’s Knightsbridge landmark, the property has 50 rooms and suites alongside private residences. Its red-brick-banded exterior answers Mayfair’s historic façades, while the interiors lean into rich contemporary craft: de Gournay wallpapers, lacquered finishes, marble, polished timber and technology handled with a quiet residential touch. The result feels more like an art-filled private house than a conventional London lobby.

The dining line-up has been recast around several distinct moods. Atrium Restaurant serves contemporary European cooking through the day, Mazarine brings a refined French sensibility, Esmeralda’s adds a jazz-bar atmosphere, and Hanover Bar crowns the building with panoramic rooftop views and polished cocktails. The scale feels deliberately intimate, more private club than hotel concourse.

Below street level, The Spa & Wellness forms one of the property’s strongest signatures, with treatment rooms, vitality pools, experience showers, a 25-metre swimming pool and a fitness centre. For a central London stay, the appeal lies in the contrast: immediate access to designer shopping, major galleries, auction previews and Mayfair dining, softened by a calm, design-led interior world and a notably serious wellness floor. Its compact footprint also suits Mayfair’s art calendar, where gallery visits and auctions can frame a stay.

highlights: Dramatic Mallorcan headland retreat with secluded coves, chef-led dining and sea-view wellness
description:
Mandarin Oriental, Mallorca brings the brand to Punta Negra, a rocky peninsula in Calvià facing the Balearic Sea and the marina life of nearby Puerto Portals. Palma’s galleries, cathedral and old-town lanes are within easy reach, but the immediate impression is coastal and elemental: Aleppo pines, carved stone paths, sea terraces and small coves below the headland.

The 131 rooms and suites include a collection of suites, casitas, plunge-pool accommodations and rooftop suites with private pools, giving the resort a residential rhythm rather than a single hotel-block feel. Contemporary Mediterranean design draws on local craft, hand-laid stone, warm timber, pale fabrics and artworks placed throughout the gardens and public spaces, keeping the mood polished but strongly connected to Mallorca’s materials and light. Many spaces are oriented to the horizon, making sea and sky part of the architecture.

Dining is unusually broad for the scale. MATSUHISA brings Nobu Matsuhisa’s Japanese-Peruvian cooking to the island; Leña by Dani García adds a fire-led steakhouse character; Jacinta looks to Mexican flavours; LEPPOC works between Mediterranean and Levantine influences; SOBRETAULA offers alfresco tapas and cava; and Thalos gives the poolside scene a Greek-accented ease.

The wellness offering includes nine treatment cabins, couples’ suites, thermal experiences, steam rooms, cold plunges, aromatherapy showers, indoor and outdoor pools, a children’s pool and a fitness centre. With Puerto Portals, Palma and the southwest coast close by, the resort reads as a polished seaside base for beach days, boating, dining and a more secluded version of the Mallorcan summer. Terraces, coves and garden paths keep the sea close, even when the day is centred on the spa or restaurants.

highlights: Historic Altstadt grande dame with rooftop city views and Japanese-Peruvian dining
description:
Mandarin Oriental, Munich stands on Neuturmstrasse in Altstadt-Lehel, tucked behind the city’s most walkable historic core. Marienplatz, the Hofbräuhaus, Maximilianstrasse, the Bavarian State Opera and the boutiques of the old town sit within easy reach, making the hotel especially well placed for culture, shopping and Munich’s ceremonial streetscape. The location is central, but the side-street approach keeps arrivals pleasingly discreet.

The building has a layered history, beginning as the 19th-century Centralsäle before its later conversion into a hotel. Today, the 73 rooms and suites balance that discreet heritage with a cleaner contemporary finish, following a substantial refurbishment of the guest accommodation. The atmosphere is smaller and more club-like than Munich’s palace hotels, with polished service spaces, warm materials and a sense of privacy that suits its Altstadt setting.

Matsuhisa Munich is the headline restaurant, bringing Nobu Matsuhisa’s Japanese-Peruvian repertoire to the city in an elegant dining room. The Munich Sushi Club, The Lounge and Ory broaden the culinary rhythm from sushi and light dishes to afternoon tea, cocktails and late-evening drinks, while the seasonal rooftop Terrace gives the hotel one of the more prized summer perches in the old town.

Facilities are compact rather than resort-like, centred on a 24-hour fitness centre and wellness support through the on-property Amour Fou Spa de Beauté. The draw is the address and the hotel’s intimate grand-hotel feel: a quietly glamorous base for the Residenz, opera, museums, beer halls and luxury shopping, with rooftop views that soften the city’s formal stone façades. Its personality rests in that tension between historic shell, Far East inflection and Munich’s polished civic confidence.

highlights: Earth-sheltered bayfront suites and pool villas above wild Messinian coast and olive groves
description:
Mandarin Oriental, Costa Navarino is set above Navarino Bay in Messenia, where the southwest Peloponnese drops into the Ionian Sea. The resort is part of the wider Costa Navarino destination, close to historic Pylos, sheltered coves, golf courses and the Navarino Agora, yet its own mood is quieter: low-slung architecture, sea-facing terraces and slopes planted with native Mediterranean greenery.

The 99 accommodations are arranged as 51 suites and 48 villas, many with private pools or generous outdoor terraces. Rather than imposing itself on the hillside, the design is embedded into the land with planted roofs, stone, terrazzo, rattan textures and pale interiors that keep attention on the water. Every stay category is shaped around views, space and a strong indoor-outdoor rhythm, with the bay almost always in sight.

Dining stretches across several concepts. Oliviera interprets Greek cooking with a view over the bay; Pizza Sapienza by Daniele Cason adds a casual Italian note; Tahir brings Levantine flavours; Brasserie de la Bay offers modern French cooking; and Ormos Beach Club, the Private Kitchen and Three Admirals Lounge cover seaside lunches, private dining, drinks and relaxed evening rituals.

The spa is a major signature, with an indoor pool, hammam, treatment spaces and a wellness approach rooted in the surrounding landscape. Outdoor pools, beach access, tennis, fitness classes, water-based activities and access to Costa Navarino’s golf infrastructure make the resort well suited to active coastal stays. Its distinction lies in the combination of Mandarin Oriental polish with a subdued, earth-toned interpretation of the Messinian coast. The nearby Agora adds restaurants, shops and an open-air cinema without disturbing the resort’s hushed bayfront character.
